extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph), including how to assess support for species, genus, amended claims, and means-plus-function limitations. Intended to direct examiners (and inform practitioners) on producing and responding to rejections and on entitlement to earlier filing/priority dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession test / objective standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must "convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention, and that the invention, in that context, is whatever is now claimed." (Vas‑Cath). Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, or by showing the invention was "ready for patenting." (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claims to a species
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim drawn to a species, the specification must provide sufficient disclosure (e.g., reduction to practice, drawings, identifying characteristics) to show possession of that species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of a method of making plus function may be insufficient in unpredictable arts; where the process has actually produced the product, written description for product‑by‑process claims is clearly satisfied. Conception that lacks structural specificity (e.g., defining a gene only by a principal biological property) is inadequate. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claims to a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by (i) sufficient description of a representative number of species (including actual reduction to practice or drawings), (ii) disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure or physical/chemical properties), (iii) functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, or (iv) a combination of such identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is substantial variation within a genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. In unpredictable arts, one species often will not support a broadly claimed genus without a demonstrated structure‑function correlation (AbbVie; Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of "representative number of species"
rubrics_metrics.description: "A 'representative number of species' means that the species which are adequately described are representative of the entire genus."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative disclosure need not provide individual support for every species; e.g., in molecular biology disclosure of an amino acid sequence can reasonably convey possession of the genus of nucleic acids encoding it because the genetic code is known. But where members vary widely and art is unpredictable, more species disclosure or correlation is needed. (In re Bell; In re Baird).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure‑function correlation as support for genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable structure‑function correlation disclosed by the inventor or known in the art can support a functionally defined genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such correlations may be established in the specification or be known in the art at filing; where established, they can permit broader genus claims even if only limited species are disclosed. Lack of correlation in unpredictable arts undermines genus support (AbbVie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the originally filed disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and to be entitled to an earlier filing/priority date), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Inherency requires that the missing matter is necessarily present and recognized by skilled artisans, not mere possibilities (In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite elements described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential or critical in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting an element described as essential can render a claim unsupported and require rejection. Courts have invalidated claims broadened by omitting elements the specification treated as critical. (Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's initial burden and presumption of adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary; the examiner has the initial burden to present a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must present by a preponderance of evidence/reasoning why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the claimed invention in the disclosure (Wertheim; In re Marzocchi). A mere general allegation (e.g., "unpredictability in the art") is insufficient without factual reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a written description rejection statement
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express factual findings that (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized possession of the claimed invention in view of the filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple statement identifying where support is not apparent may suffice for new/amended claims, but broad conclusory statements are inadequate. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the original disclosure, mindful of the prohibition on adding new matter. (MPEP §2163.04(I)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment upon applicant reply / whole‑record review
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must re‑determine patentability and whether the written description requirement is satisfied in view of the whole record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates satisfaction, do not repeat the rejection. If not, fully respond to rebuttal arguments and analyze any affidavits in the next Office action. (In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of means‑/step‑plus‑function limitations due to insufficient corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A means‑(or step‑) plus‑function claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA sixth paragraph) must be supported by corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification that perform the claimed function; otherwise the limitation is indefinite and lacks adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure renders the limitation indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) and also fails the written description requirement because it covers all ways of performing the function and indicates lack of possession. (In re Donaldson; see MPEP §2181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments that change claim scope require support
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to claim scope after filing (broadening or narrowing, altering numerical ranges, or using terminology not synonymous with original disclosure) commonly raise written description issues and each resulting claim limitation must be supported by the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of a limitation can suggest lack of possession of a broader invention, particularly where the specification described the omitted element as the only possible location or essential. Examples: Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder. When appropriate, suggest supported amendments but avoid adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on benefit/priority/parent filing dates
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the benefit of an earlier U.S. or foreign filing date (35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, 386), the subject matter of the claim must be described in the earlier application in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner initially must present evidence/reasoning why the earlier disclosure does not support the later claim. Applicant should specifically point out original support for amendments. Cases: Tronzo; In re Scheiber; In re Gosteli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims may still lack written description
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support if it defines the invention in purely functional language without sufficient identification of how the function is performed, or if a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure describes only a narrow species with no evidence the genus was contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if claim language appears verbatim in the specification, indistinct or mere words may not satisfy the requirement; the specification must describe the claimed invention so one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed (Enzo Biochem; Ariad en banc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence types that can establish possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession can be shown by actual reduction to practice, by disclosure showing invention was "ready for patenting" (e.g., drawings, structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These descriptive means include words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas; reliance on patents and printed publications in the art can help determine maturity of the art and level of skill. (Pfaff; Lockwood; Eli Lilly).
